opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the cleanest way to see it is in terms of how much signal you get per example. When you train on synthetic outputs, the teacher generates a sequence and you do supervised fine-tuning on it. So you're getting one sampled token at each position, basically a one-hot target. With logits, you get the teacher's whole distribution at every position. You learn not just what the teacher said, but what else it considered plausible and how confident it was. That's the old "dark knowledge" idea from Hinton, and for language models it matters a lot. You get much denser supervision, so you often need far fewer examples for the same quality.

That said, logits aren't free. You need white-box access to the teacher, and ideally a shared tokenizer, which rules out a lot of practical setups. If you're distilling from an API model, synthetic data is basically all you have. Storing full distributions over a big vocabulary is also expensive, so people truncate to the top-k, and that loses some of the benefit.

What I actually find more important than logits versus samples is *whose* outputs you're training on. With standard distillation, either kind, the student only learns on sequences the teacher produced. But at inference time, the student generates its own sequences, makes its own mistakes, and ends up in states the teacher never showed it. That's the train-inference mismatch, essentially exposure bias. That was a big motivation for our work on on-policy distillation. You let the student generate, and then you ask the teacher for feedback on the student's own outputs, ideally token-level logits. That combines the dense signal of logits with on-policy data, and it gave much bigger gains than just switching the loss or adding more teacher samples. It also connects nicely to RL: it looks a lot like RL with a very dense reward from the teacher.

So my rough heuristic: if you only have black-box access, synthetic data is fine and scales well, especially with good filtering. If you have the teacher's weights, use the logits. And if you can afford it, do it on the student's own samples. That's usually where most of the value is.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data can be fine when only black-box access is available, but it does not state that synthetic-output distillation can outperform teacher-logit distillation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because people tend to treat these as two completely different things, and I'd argue they're really points on the same spectrum. When you do logit distillation, you're matching the full distribution the teacher puts over the vocabulary at every position. When you do what people call synthetic data distillation, or sequence-level distillation, you're sampling a sequence from the teacher and training on it with next-token prediction. That second thing is really just a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate of the first. So the question isn't logits versus samples in some fundamental sense, it's about how much signal you get per unit of compute and what the data distribution looks like.

Where logits are genuinely valuable is in the information density. Instead of a single hard token, the student sees the teacher's entire ranking over alternatives: what it almost said, what it considered plausible. That's a lot of bits per position, and for smaller students that richer gradient matters a lot. The classic result, going back to Hinton, is that this dark knowledge is what lets a small model pick up the teacher's inductive biases rather than just memorizing outputs.

The catch is that logit distillation has real constraints. You need the teacher and student to share a tokenizer, or you need to do some painful alignment. You need access to the teacher's logits, which rules out most API models. And more subtly, you have to decide whose sequences you compute those logits on. If you compute them on a fixed dataset, the student never sees the states it would actually reach when generating on its own, and you get that train-inference mismatch. That's the thing that motivated our on-policy distillation work: have the student generate, then get the teacher's feedback on those tokens. Once you do that, the distinction gets blurry again, because now you're using logits but on student-sampled data.

Synthetic outputs have their own case. They're portable: you can distill from anything you can query. They're reusable: one expensive generation can be filtered, reranked, and trained on many times, by many students. And crucially, you can apply quality control. With rejection sampling or verifier filtering, the synthetic data can actually be better than the teacher's average behavior, because you're keeping the best of N. You can't do that with raw logits in the same way. The teacher's distribution is the teacher's distribution, including its mistakes.

So the way I'd judge it in practice: if you own the teacher, share the vocabulary, and the student is small and capacity-constrained, the per-token distribution is giving you a real advantage and you should use it, ideally on student-generated or at least mixed-policy data. If the teacher is behind an API, or you want to reuse the data across many runs, or the task has a verifier, synthetic data with filtering wins, and the gap closes a lot as the student gets larger because a capable student can infer a lot from hard labels. The mistake I see is people assuming one dominates. It almost always comes down to the specific compute budget and what you're actually trying to transfer.

r001.rationale: The response says filtered synthetic data can be better than the teacher’s average behavior and that synthetic data with filtering wins in some settings, directly indicating it can outperform logit-based distillation.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is that a synthetic output tells you what the teacher chose, whereas logits tell you something about the alternatives it considered. If two tokens are almost equally likely, you lose that information when you train only on the sampled token. So logits can give you a richer learning signal per example.

But that doesn’t automatically make them more valuable in practice. Synthetic outputs are easy to collect, you can use them with an API model, and you can spend your budget generating more diverse examples. Logits require access to the teacher’s distribution, and differences in tokenization can make them harder to use.

The comparison I’d want is under a fixed budget: does the richer supervision buy you more than additional synthetic examples? And I’d also look at where the training sequences come from. Giving teacher feedback on sequences the student actually generates can address mistakes that wouldn’t appear in teacher-generated data. So I’d judge the supervision signal and the data distribution together, rather than treating logits as inherently better.

r001.rationale: The response says logits are not automatically more valuable and asks whether richer supervision beats generating more examples, but it does not state that synthetic-output distillation can sometimes outperform logit distillation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main advantage of teacher logits is that they tell you more than just which token the teacher chose. They tell you which alternatives it considered plausible and how it distributed probability across them. With synthetic outputs, you get a sampled trajectory, and you train the student to imitate that trajectory. That’s useful, but it discards some of the teacher’s information.

That doesn’t mean logits are automatically more valuable in practice. You have to account for the cost of accessing and storing them, whether the teacher and student share a tokenizer, and what data you’re distilling on. A well-chosen set of synthetic examples can be more useful than logits on examples that don’t match the task.

So I’d compare them under a fixed budget: how much does each improve the student on the capabilities you care about? Logits provide a richer training signal, but data quality and coverage can matter more than the format of that signal.

r001.rationale: It says well-chosen synthetic examples can be more useful than teacher logits on examples that do not match the task, communicating that synthetic-output distillation can sometimes outperform logit-based distillation.
